title: Knowledge Check 2: Lessons 6-10
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 6-10 of the hermes-consultant-intermediate series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: What number defines the estimate for a multi-week delivery?
options: The sum of all task effort across the plan
The longest chain of dependent work
The average of the three-point ranges
The total number of scoped tasks
questions.explanation: The end date is set by the longest chain of dependent work, because parallel workstreams run at the same time rather than one after another.

questions.question: Where do fixed-duration gates like a security review belong in the estimate?
options: Hidden inside the build task they affect
Left out until the build is complete
Averaged into the total effort
On the critical path as their own items
questions.explanation: A gate runs on its owner's calendar and cannot be compressed by effort, so it must appear as a fixed-duration item on the critical path.

questions.question: How should the ongoing operation of an agent be priced?
options: As part of the one-time build total
As a per-run cost only, with no ongoing rate
As a weekly rate kept apart from the build
As a fixed fee paid once at handover
questions.explanation: The build is a one-time total while the ongoing operation recurs weekly, so it is priced as a rate plus a per-run cost.

questions.question: What must a seam between two owners contain to stay durable?
options: A verbal agreement that both owners renew each morning
What it delivers, needs, and its acceptance bar
The names of both owners and their roles
A status flag updated by the upstream owner
questions.explanation: A seam is an interface, and it stays usable only when both owners can read what the piece delivers, what it needs, and the bar it must meet.

questions.question: When does work need a durable team rather than a spawned parallel child?
options: When the parent needs a fast reasoning answer to continue
When the subtask is short and self-contained
When it must survive restarts and cross owners
When the result stays in one parent's context
questions.explanation: Durable team work crosses owner boundaries, survives restarts, and must be findable later, while a spawned child answers once and vanishes with its parent.

questions.question: What is a delivery lead's own deliverable?
options: The most difficult piece of the production work
A personal sign-off on every finished task
A weekly status update for the client
The team's shape and the integrity of its seams
questions.explanation: A lead decomposes, routes, and watches the seams, and steps out of execution so the seams get the attention the team depends on.

questions.question: What makes a pilot a hypothesis test rather than a demo?
options: It uses clean synthetic data to ensure success
It states a measurable claim before building
It shows the client every feature of the tool
It delivers the whole engagement at no cost
questions.explanation: A demo produces a feeling, while a pilot converts by testing a measurable claim that can be confirmed or falsified before it is built.

questions.question: What should the pilot's slice be?
options: The whole problem, so the client sees it work
The easiest part, so the pilot cannot fail
A representative slice on the real data
A synthetic sample chosen to flatter the tool
questions.explanation: The slice must be representative of real data and failure modes yet bounded, so it proves the mechanism without becoming the delivery.

questions.question: When should the conversion gate be set?
options: After the pilot succeeds and the proof is clear
Only if the client later asks to pay for more
At the very end, during contract negotiation
Before the pilot starts, with terms sketched
questions.explanation: After the pilot succeeds the power shifts to the client, so the gate and its terms must be agreed before the proof exists.

questions.question: Why must a quality system at scale run both a gate and a sample?
options: A gate catches regressions caused by a change, while a sample catches drift
A gate catches drift over time, while a sample catches change-driven regressions
A gate replaces the golden set, while a sample replaces the need for a gate
A gate screens each live output, while a sample audits the golden set's cases
questions.explanation: A change-triggered gate and a human sample of the live stream cover opposite failures: what a change broke and what drifted with no change at all. Running only one leaves half the estate unverified.

questions.question: When a golden set case fails, what is the correct first response?
options: Rewrite the expected output to match what the system currently does so the gate turns green
Remove the failing case from the set so it stops blocking the planned release
Decide whether the system regressed or the world changed before touching it
Lower the pass bar slightly until the failing case passes again
questions.explanation: The set holds the quality bar, so a failure is a question to answer, not a bar to move. Moving the expected output to match the system deletes the record of what correct used to be.

questions.question: A failing gate is triaged as one of three diagnoses. Which set is correct?
options: A real regression, a stale reference, or a flaky test, each needing its own fix
A real regression, a capacity shortage, or a billing error, each needing its own fix
A blocked run, an expired key, or a delivery failure, each needing its own fix
A scope issue, a schedule issue, or a provider issue, each needing its own fix
questions.explanation: Naming the diagnosis is the whole skill because the fix differs: fix the system for a regression, update the case for stale reference, repair the test for a flaky gate.

questions.question: Why route mechanical work off the model and into a script?
options: A deterministic script costs nothing per run and cannot drift in judgment
A script produces genuinely higher-quality reasoning than a model on routine work
A script lets the whole fleet skip the need for any health signal at all
A script removes the need to model the weekly burn of the whole estate
questions.explanation: The cheapest reliable run is the one that never calls a model, and a deterministic check is the one component that cannot quietly change its own mind. Mechanical work gains nothing from reasoning.

questions.question: An unpinned unattended job would inherit a changed global default. What is the correct posture?
options: Inherit the new default and keep running so the fleet stays alive
Skip the run, make no inference call, and alert once
Retry against the new default until it succeeds or the budget runs out
Run on both the old and the new default and compare the cost
questions.explanation: An unattended job should fail closed: skip and alert rather than guess and spend. This protects both the budget and the operator's honesty when a change was never meant for the fleet.

questions.question: Where should redundancy be placed in an agent estate?
options: On every job equally, so that no single run in the estate can ever miss
On the cheapest and most frequent jobs, since those fire the greatest number of times
On the inference path, and only where the cost of a missed run is high
On the data sources, since those are the widest dependency the fleet shares
questions.explanation: The one truly shared component is the inference path, so redundancy belongs there. Redundancy is insurance priced against the cost of a lost run, spent only where failure is expensive.
